text: The assembly will hear an address by His
Excellency Matthew Cooper Whale, Prime
Minister of Solomon Islands.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President, Secretary General of the
United Nations, excellencies,
distinguished delegates,
I stand before this assembly conscious
that I speak on behalf of a nation and
the people whose future is being shaped
in holes like this one.
I bring warm greetings from the people
and government of Solomon Islands, a
nation of nearly a thousand islands
stretching across as many miles of the
blue Pacific.
Our people hold the same hopes as people
in every land to live in peace and to
raise their children in dignity.
Mr. President, I congratulate you on
your election and assure you of the full
support of Solomon Islands. I also
commend your predecessor for her
determined leadership of the 80th
session.
I pay special tribute to Secretary
General Antonio Gutirez as he takes part
in his final debate in office. Mr.
Secretary General, you have been a true
champion of multilateralism and of small
island developing states. Your
unwavering advocacy on climate action
and your repeated visits to our region
told the world a simple truth that the
Pacific matters and that our challenges
and how the world responds to them
remain a litmus test for this
organization and for us all.
We meet at a time when multilateralism
is under serious strain and when the
notion that might is right appears to be
making a return. Yet we continue to
gather in forums and dialogues around
the world and here in the general
assembly, the pinnacle of
multilateralism.
That in itself is course for hope.
Mr. President, for my people, what is
said in this hall is measured not in
declarations but in results. Classrooms
with teachers and books, clinics with
medicines, roads that reach markets and
villages that thrive. That is the lens
through which Solomon Islands engages
with the world.
My government is delivering a program of
national transformation.
We are providing universal free
education so that no child is turned
away from school because their family
cannot afford the fees. We are
strengthening our health system with a
renewed focus on tackling the scourge of
non-communicable diseases,
eradicating malaria, and building a new
national referral hospital.
We are prioritizing energy and other
transformative infrastructure, expanding
roads, ports, airports, and
telecommunications
to connect our scattered islands into
one national economy.
We are reforming our public finance
systems so that every dollar delivers
for our people and we are pursuing
constitutional amendments to strengthen
and stabilize our democracy.
This is the agenda by which our people
will judge my government.
Mr. President, over the past year, the
international community has faced many
challenges.
Protracted armed conflicts and energy
crisis and disruptions to global trade
have been compounded by destabilization
orchestrated by those who pursue their
own selfish ambitions.
For small island economies, these are
not distant events.
Every rise in the price of fuel is felt
in the cost of shipping.
electricity, food, and essential
services, placing a heavy burden on
communities that have no buffer against
external shocks.
These tensions confirm what Solomman
Islands has long understood.
Peace and security are inseparable from
development. Neither can be secured
without the other.
There are no winners in war, only
graves, orphans, and the long labor of
rebuilding what conflict has torn down.
There is no substitute for dialogue,
diplomacy, and peaceful negotiation.
Solomon Islands calls on all parties to
armed conflicts to protect civilians and
return to the negotiating table and act
in full respect of international law.
And it is why the world needs a
stronger, more agile United Nations, one
equipped to respond to the realities of
today.
Mr. President, the Pacific faces a grave
and growing threat. Transnational
criminal networks are using our ocean as
a highway for illicit drugs, undermining
our sovereignty and national security,
destroying young lives and tearing at
the fabric of our communities.
Behind every statistic stands a family,
a community, a young life robbed of its
promise.
We will not allow criminal networks to
profit from the vulnerability of our
people.
We are amending our dangerous drugs act
to in introduce stiffer penalties as a
deterrent and we are strengthening law
enforcement to prevent and detect these
crimes and to hold perpetrators
accountable. In August this year,
Solomon Islands succeeded to the UN
convention against transnational
organized crime, a clear demonstration
of our resolve to confront this threat.
These are costly and demanding
undertakings and no Pacific country can
win this fight alone. We call for
stronger international cooperation,
greater information sharing, sustained
investment in the capacity of our law
enforcement agencies and the support uh
for prevention uh and rehabilitation.
Our vision of a peaceful and secure
Pacific extends beyond transnational
crime. As enshrined in the Ocean of
Peace Declaration, our region must
remain free of nuclear weapons and free
from destabilizing external influence.
In keeping with that vision, my
government has proposed a treaty that
would bind Pacific Island countries and
like-minded partners to a firm shared
commitment to keep the Pacific an ocean
of peace.
Mr. President,
artificial intelligence and emerging
technologies present both unprecedented
opportunities and serious risks. They
can accelerate sustainable development,
transform education and health care,
strengthen disaster preparedness, and
open new economic pathways for
developing countries.
But a widening digital divide threatens
to leave developing countries further
behind. For my government, digital
transformation is not about technology
for its own sake. It is about connecting
our scattered islands and opening the
modern economy to every Solomon
Islander. The completion of 161
telecommunication towers across the
country will lift national broadband
coverage from 56 to 86%.
Expanding access to information,
education, and digital financial
services.
The benefits of AI must be shared by
all, Mr. president not concentrated
among a few. Its risks, including its
use for non- peaceful purposes, must be
governed by all, not left to a few.
Solomon Islands therefore recognizes the
need for an inclusive and transparent
international governance framework on
AI.
Mr. President, year after year, Pacific
leaders have stood at this podium and
urged the world to act on climate
change. And yet global action continues
to fall short of what the science
demands.
For every passing COP, the impacts grow
more severe.
Our islands are being lost to the sea.
Disasters are more frequent and more
devastating.
Food and sec water security is under
threat. And communities are being forced
from their ancestral lands.
Solomon Islands knows this reality
firsthand.
This year, tropical cyclone miler, a
category 5 storm, tore through our
communities, destroying homes, schools,
infrastructure, and livelihoods.
My government has just approved US 9.38
million for shelter recovery. That is
money our essential services urgently
need now diverted to deal with the
impacts of this climate extreme.
Like many Pacific Island countries, we
are trapped in a relentless cycle of
response, recovery, and rebuilding.
This is not sustainable,
nor is it just. My people did the least
to cause this crisis, yet they pay its
earliest and heaviest price. That is the
moral ledger that lies before this
assembly.
Last year, the International Court of
Justice confirmed in its landmark
advisory opinion that states have legal
obligations to protect the climate
system.
Major emitters must make deep emission
cuts and trans transition away from
fossil fuels.
Climate finance, including support for
loss and damage, must be grant-based and
channeled through our national budget
systems.
Project-based financing of climate
action is unsustainable and out of step
with the scale of a crisis we did the
least to cause.
Vulnerable countries should not have to
choose between climate action and
educating our children, caring for the
sick, or securing food and water. Yet,
that is the choice we face with every
dollar we spend. We therefore call for
the full capitalization of the Pacific
Resilience Facility and an ambitious and
timely third replenishment of the Green
Climate Fund.
Our region has long led on climate
action and we will continue to lead. The
pre-COP 31 meeting to be hosted in the
Pacific by Australia in partnership with
Fiji and Tuvalu will bring the reality
of climate change directly into the
heart of the global process.
I call on all parties and partners to
come to that meeting and to COP 31 with
stronger commitments and concrete
action. The communities on the front
line of the climate crisis deserve
nothing less.
Mr. President, Solomon Islands welcomes
the convening of the second high level
meeting on sea level rise and the
adoption of the first political
declaration on sea level rise. Every day
our people are defending their
coastlines, strengthening their
resilience, protecting their food and
water security and their cultural
heritage. and where there is no other
choice, relocating.
But we cannot do this alone.
I call on this assembly to match the
courage of our Pacific communities with
collective international resolve to
scale up adaptation and res resilience
finance and to support communities
facing climate mobility needs.
Solomon Islands reaffirm reaffirms
that maritime boundaries once
established and deposited in accordance
with UNCLO together with the rights and
entitlements that flow from them shall
continue to apply notwithstanding any
physical changes caused by climate
change related sea level rise.
Sir, the ocean is not simply a resource.
It is our identity, our heritage, and
our future. It sustains our livelihoods,
our culture, and our economy. We do not
own the ocean. We belong to it. We hold
it in solemn trust for generations yet
to be born.
Yet our ability to benefit fully from
our own ocean is undermined by illegal,
unreported and unregulated fishing which
costs our region US30 million every
year. Solomon Islands is fighting back,
working with the Foreign Fisheries
Agency and partners including Australia,
France, New Zealand, and the US to
strengthen surveillance and enforcement
across our waters.
Mr. President, the SDG14 remains among
the least funded of all the sustainable
development goals. With just four years
left until 2030, the fourth UN Ocean
Conference must raise the bar on ocean
finance and secure the oceanceans's
place in the development agenda beyond
Solomon Islands welcomes the entry into
force of the BBNJ agreement and the
preparations for the first conference of
the parties in January.
We look to that conference to establish
without delay the secretariat and the
institutional arrangements to implement
the agreement.
Plastic pollution is poisoning our ocean
and our food. As negotiations resume in
Bangkok, Solomon Islands calls for an
ambitious, legally binding treaty that
addresses the full cycle of plastics
from production to disposal.
Mr. President, our people are our
greatest asset. With more than half of
our population under the age of 25, my
government is prioritizing legal
frameworks that empower young people,
advance gender equality, and strengthen
the protection of women and children
against domestic violence. We welcome
global progress in advancing the rights
and full participation of women and
persons with disabilities in the
economy, and Solomon Islands is
committed to accelerating that progress
at home.
There can be no sustainable development
without equal opportunity for all.
Mr. President, our development
partnerships play an indispensable role
in expanding infrastructure, maritime
connectivity, health and education, and
in improving the lives of Solomon
Islanders. I thank the governments and
peoples of Australia, China, Japan, New
Zealand, the Republic of Korea and the
US as well as the EU for their
contributions to our national
development.
South South Corporation remains an
important complement to ODA.
Partnerships among developing countries
have enabled us to share expertise,
technology, innovation and practical
solutions suited to our circumstances.
The support of Papu Guinea, Indonesia,
India and our Pacific family embodies
the true spirit of South South
solidarity and we value it deeply. We
also acknowledge the partnership of
multilateral organizations,
NOS's and the private sector in
supporting development work in Solomon
Islands. At home, my government is
working hand in hand with churches to
build stronger, more inclusive
communities.
Cooperation and partnership at every
level and across borders are critical to
nation building and my government
remains fully committed to them.
Mr. President, as a small island
developing state, our vulnerability
remains a fundamental reality.
This a single natural disaster can erase
years of investment and progress and
push the nation backwards.
The multi-dimensional
vulnerability index captures the special
circumstances of of SIDS in a way that
income measures alone does not.
We call on international financial
institutions to in integrate the MVI
into their financing decisions for SIDS
without further delay.
Mr. President, last year the world's the
world spent more than $3 trillion on its
militaries.
That is more than 16 times all ODA.
In less than 18 days, the world spends
more on arms than developed countries
provide in a full year of climate
finance. In a in the same year that
military spending reached its highest
share of global output since 2009,
development aid had its steepest fall on
record. Bilateral aid to the least
developed countries fell by a quarter.
This imbalance must be corrected.
Redirecting even a small share of this
spending would fully capitalize the
Pacific Resilience Facility and the loss
and damage fund, secure the Green
Climate Fund's third replenishment, and
meet ODA targets.
The resources exist. What is missing is
the will, and the time to act is now.
Sir, Solman Islands is due to graduate
from least developed country status in
As part of our preparations,
my government is pursuing an ambitious
and proactive agenda that uses public
private partnerships to unlock
investments in transformative projects,
special economic zones and key sectors,
a second tuna canary at Beina Harour,
upgraded airports, agricultural
treatment facilities to support trade,
and expanded road networks and maritime
ports will shift the trajectory. of our
economy.
At the same time, my government is
strengthening our financial institutions
and frameworks to improve revenue
collection and accountability so that we
can sustain our development priorities.
These reforms reflect our commitment to
a strong and resilient economy that
delivers decentralized people centered
development across the country. Our
ambition is clear to graduate from LDC
status with confidence to strengthen the
foundations of our economy and to ensure
that development delivers lasting
opportunities for every Solomon
Islander.
Mr. President, as the UN marks it its
81st anniversary, it must continue to
evolve to meet today's challenges while
remaining faithful to its founding
principles.
The UN80 reform process must strengthen
the organization's effectiveness and
relevance without diminishing its
presence, services or support
in the most vulnerable regions where
assistance is needed most. Reform must
enhance delivery,
not reduce it.
The UN is not perfect, but it remains
the cornerstone of multilateral
diplomacy and the indispensable platform
through which nations preserve peace,
advance sustainable development, uphold
international law, and protect human
rights.
Solomon Islands looks to the next
secretary general to lead with vision
and to ensure that the secretariat is
accountable to all member states serving
the interests of small and large states
on an equal footing.
Mr. President Solomon Islands reiterates
its support for comprehensive reform of
the Security Council to make it more
representative, transparent,
accountable, and reflective of today's
realities.
A council with a dedicated seat for
small island developing states would
strengthen the legitimacy and
effectiveness of the entire multilateral
system.
The veto is a relic of 1945.
Too often, it has been used to shield
violations of international law and to
entrench the double standards that fuel
conflict. At a minimum, the veto must
never again be used in situations of
genocide, crimes against humanity, or
war crimes. Ultimately, it should be
abolished.
Mr. President, it is with great pride
that Solomon Islands is again
contributing personnel to UN
peacekeeping in South Sudan.
Despite our small size, our
participation reaffirms our enduring
commitment to the charter, to
international peace and security, and to
the noble work of peacekeepers serving
communities affected by conflict. I
thank our partners including Australia
and the UN police for their support.
Solman Islands looks forward to
increasing its peacekeeping contribution
in the coming year.
Mr. President, leaving no one behind
demands that we complete the unfinished
work of decolonization.
Solomon Islands reaffirms its
long-standing support for the right to
self-determination of the Kanak people
of New Calonia and the Maui Nui people
of French Polynesia.
The UN decolonization process must offer
more than hope. It must provide
practical pathways to the full
emancipation of peoples in
non-self-governing territories and to
their freedom to determine their own
political future and development
aspirations.
In the same spirit, I turn to West
Papua, whose people are our Melnishian
brothers and sisters.
Solomon Islands respects the sovereignty
and territorial integrity of the
Republic of Indonesia and we value our
friendship with its government and
people.
Yet, it is precisely because of that
friendship that we speak with Kanda.
Reports of human rights violations in
West Papua have persisted for far too
long. They must be independently
verified, not left in dispute.
We therefore renew the call of Pacific
Islands forum leaders for the government
of Indonesia
to facilitate without further delay the
long- awaited visit of the UN High
Commissioner for Human Rights to West
Papua. Such a visit is an act of
confidence between friends and an
affirmation that there is nothing to
hide and there is nothing to fear from
the light.
Mr. President, in closing, the
challenges of our time demand renewed
solidarity,
stronger multilateralism,
and genuine commitment to the principles
of the UN charter. But institutions do
not have hearts. People do.
Charters do not keep the peace. The men
and women who honor them do. Beyond
every declaration and commitment, each
of us carries a profound responsibility
to be agents of peace, champions of
goodwill, and keepers of the fragile
bonds of friendship among nations. The
world has never needed that spirit more
than it does today.
Mr. President, permit me a word from the
Christian faith that has shaped my
people. Our constitution was established
under the guiding hand of God by a
people conscious of our common destiny.
We believe that is true not only of
Solomon Islands but of this whole family
of nations. We live in a time when
division has become the calling card of
the day. Nations are sorted into camps.
Neighbors are asked to choose sides.
Small states are too often treated as
prizes to be won rather than partners to
be heard.
But the destiny of nations does not
finally rest in this general assembly,
nor in any capital, however powerful.
King Solomon, among the wisest rulers of
antiquity, wrote, "There are many
devices in a man's heart. Nevertheless,
the council of the Lord shall stand."
that truth does not make us passive. It
makes us humble and it makes us
accountable. So I call on my fellow
fellow leaders to do three things.
First, let us ask for wisdom before we
ask for advantage.
When Solomon was offered anything he
wished,
he did not ask for riches or long life
or the defeat of his enemies. He asked
for an understanding heart so that he
might judge his people well. I can think
of no better prayer for every leader in
this room.
Second, let us stay at the table. The
same king taught that in the multitude
of counselors
there is safety.
That is the oldest case I know for what
this organization is meant to be. Many
nations large and small sitting together
because none of us sees far enough
alone.
Third, let us measure greatness rightly.
Righteousness exalts the nation. Not its
arsenal, not its alliances, but its
justice. How it treats the poor, the
displaced, and the small.
Powers rise and powers fall. The
purposes of God endure. Let us choose
cooperation over division, dialogue over
confrontation,
peace over hostility, and action over
inaction. And let us lead as people who
know we will answer for it one day.
Our national moto teaches us that to
lead is to serve. In that spirit of
service, Solomman Island stands ready to
do its part as a willing partner and a
committed member of this assembly.
May God bless our shared family of
nations. Thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the prime minister of Solomon
Island.
